Article Title: Quote of the day by Reid Hoffman: Go home have dinner with your family; Then, after dinner with your family, open up your laptop and get back in the shared work experience and keep working
Article Text:
What Reid Hoffman's quote means

Why LinkedIn co-founder says work-life balance is different at startups

The bigger message behind the quote

Would you close your laptop after dinner—or open it again and get back to work? LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman believes the answer can be very different when you are working at a startup. Recalling LinkedIn's early days, Reid Hoffman said employees were encouraged to go home and have dinner with their families. But the workday was not necessarily over. “Go home have dinner with your family. Then, after dinner with your family, open up your laptop and get back in the shared work experience and keep working,” Hoffman said.Simply put, Hoffman believes that building a startup often requires work beyond regular office hours. His idea was not that employees should completely avoid spending time with their families. Instead, he described an arrangement where everyone could take a break for dinner and then return to a shared online workspace later in the evening.In a Stanford discussion, Reid Hoffman explained that this was designed as a company-wide approach, rather than allowing only parents to leave early and potentially feel left out of important work.He said the goal was to give people time with their families while keeping the team focused on the work needed to build the company.Hoffman has been clear about his views on startup culture. He has argued that startups operate in a competitive environment where companies are trying to grow quickly and survive.“Work life balance is not the startup game,” he said, adding that startup work is intense. Hoffman has also argued that working at a startup is a choice and that not everyone has to choose that path.His views, however, have also sparked debate. For many workers, the idea of returning to work after dinner raises questions about personal time and the boundary between work and family life.Reid Hoffman's quote is ultimately about the level of commitment he believes is needed to build a startup. In his view, a young company competing for success cannot always follow the schedule of a regular nine-to-five job.The message is not necessarily that everyone should work after dinner. Rather, it reflects Hoffman's belief that people who choose the startup path may have to accept periods of intense work and make trade-offs that are different from those in more established companies.
Article Summary: LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman says work-life balance is different at startups. He believes that building a startup often requires work beyond regular office hours. Hoffman has also argued that working at a startup is a choice and that not everyone has to choose that path.

Article Title: America's richest techies' new status symbol is a Swiss watch, and Sam Altman ordered seven worth over $1 million with these words engraved on them
Article Text:
Sam Altman's OpenAI watch: seven made, over $1 million (Credit: Vanguart)

What's actually engraved on Sam Altman's OpenAI watch

Vanguart engraved 'SCALING' on the crown pusher and 'COMPUTE IS DESTINY' around the rotor of the OpenAI watches

Vanguart is tiny even by Swiss watchmaking standards

OpenAI's Tudor watch is the version mortals can chase

Why company-logo watches now resell above retail

Silicon Valley has run through a lot of flexes. The hoodie. The Tesla. The Cybertruck parked outside a Palo Alto bungalow worth eight figures. The latest one is smaller, quieter and sits on the wrist. It is also the most expensive thing most of these men own that is not real estate. And Sam Altman has taken it further than anyone else in tech.The OpenAI chief executive commissioned seven custom watches from Vanguart, a Swiss maker that has been around for barely eight years, according to a Wall Street Journal report. They were built for a handful of hand-picked OpenAI staff, and the engraving reads less like watchmaking and more like an in-joke from a research lab. The order was based on Vanguart's titanium Orb, a model that starts at $180,000—which puts seven of them past the million-dollar mark before customisation. Altman declined to comment through an OpenAI spokeswoman.Wind the watch and you'll find "COMPUTE IS DESTINY" running around the rotor in capitals, a line attributed to Altman himself. The crown pusher carries a single word—"SCALING". Flip it over and the caseback reads if AGI.aligned: deploy(), written in Python, rendered in colour on the movement, the way code looks inside an editor with syntax highlighting on.It also has "LIMITED OpenAI" stamped around the rim. And, there's an OpenAI logo on the dial.That last one was suggested by Axel Leuenberger, Vanguart's CEO and co-founder. Company chairman and co-founder Mehmet Koruturk told the Journal the line is about AI being put to peaceful use. OpenAI's knot logo sits at 12 o'clock as an applied, openworked piece, roughly where a brand name would normally go. Hands and hour markers glow a pale green, and the flying tourbillon spins away in the open at 6 o'clock with no dial covering it.Underneath the styling is a serious watch. The Orb runs 41mm across and 10.5mm thick in grade 5 titanium, with a movement of 395 components, 35 jewels and about 60 hours of power reserve. Switching between automatic and manual winding is done through the crown, and in automatic mode a titanium orbital mass set with a 2mm diamond circles a track on the dial side, appearing to float.Roughly a third of Vanguart's 33 employees worked on the OpenAI commission, Koruturk said. For scale: Audemars Piguet has more than 3,000 staff and turns out about 50,000 watches a year. Vanguart has made fewer than 200 in its entire existence. In the US, its ready-made pieces are sold at exactly one address—Material Good in SoHo.Hidden details are a house habit. Koruturk told the Journal the brand aims for "subtle tributes embedded for those who know where to look."Not every OpenAI watch costs as much as an apartment. Boris Power, the company's head of applied research, posted on X that Tudor—Rolex's sister brand—made 400 watches carrying the OpenAI logo on the dial, with "Good Research Takes Time" on the back, a slogan OpenAI has also printed on T-shirts.And OpenAI is far from alone. Business Insider reported that Palantir staff got a run of 468, an Uber engineer posted a model numbered 1/100, and Google's version used the Tudor Pelagos, which retails around $4,500. These aren't gifts from HR. They're organised by employee collector groups, who round up enough buyers to hit Tudor's minimum order of 40, then wait about six months. Everyone pays full retail.At Adobe, product designer Georgia Benjamin is working with British watchmaker Studio Underd0g on a 128-piece run at around $1,200 each, for employees only. Benjamin, who owns about 40 watches, described the appeal as belonging to an insider club.The secondary market has noticed. Eric Ku, co-founder of online auction house Loupe This, sold an Amazon-branded Tudor earlier this year for $8,250. A Tudor Black Bay 54 customised with Meta's logo has drawn bids as high as $10,500—a standard version with a metal bracelet retails for $4,725. Business Insider reported that a Google Tudor featuring the Chrome dinosaur went past $10,000 at auction, while an Apple "pirate" edition pulled a $13,500 bid. Ku's read is simple: collectors chase the unusual. He also warned that plenty of branded pieces flop—people sometimes just find them ugly.None of this is new territory for tech's biggest names. Mark Zuckerberg has worn a $1.3 million F.P. Journe. Altman's collection includes a Greubel Forsey that ran to roughly $650,000. What's changed is the flex itself—less about what the watch cost, more about the logo on the dial telling you where its owner works.
Article Summary: OpenAI chief executive commissioned seven custom watches from Vanguart, a Swiss maker that has been around for barely eight years. They were built for a handful of hand-picked OpenAI staff, and the engraving reads less like watchmaking and more like an in-joke.

Article Title: Datacentres have forced Ireland government to do something that has been unthinkable for over fifty years
Article Text:
Representative Image

“We’re open to that [nuclear].”

Ireland's nuclear power ban dates back decades

“Nuclear is the way to go,”

Data centres are reshaping Ireland's electricity demand

Ireland's nuclear debate faces practical questions

“We should be doing, in the 2020s, what the French did in the 1970s,”

“It takes a long time to get ready, hence we should start now,”

“I’m seeing real traction [in the UK] that could deliver quicker than you think,”

“Nuclear is certainly not something that can address any of those challenges in the next 15 to 20 years,”

“nuclear will face the same, if not more, constraints as the offshore wind industry is facing — and offshore wind doesn’t rely on importing uranium”.

Ireland still has to expand renewable electricity

“The risk is that we spend too much time debating theoretical future options while forgetting the deliverable projects that are key to unlocking lower-cost, homegrown and green power this decade and the next,”

Ireland is reconsidering its long-standing ban on nuclear power as electricity demand from data centres continues to rise. This has prompted the government to reopen a debate that had been largely closed for more than five decades. Data centres already account for nearly a quarter of the country's electricity consumption, a share that is expected to reach at least 30% by 2032.The shift marks a change in Ireland's approach to nuclear power, which has remained politically and legally off the table for decades. According to a report by The Financial Times, Taoiseach Micheál Martin recently told a business dinner,His comments came as the government faces growing pressure to expand electricity generation while meeting rising demand from data centres and other large users.Ireland first considered nuclear power during the 1973 oil shock, when the country was heavily dependent on imported energy. Plans for a nuclear plant on the south-east coast later faced strong opposition, with several high-profile protests beginning in 1978.The Three Mile Island reactor accident in the US in 1979 further turned public opinion against nuclear power.The country eventually prohibited nuclear fission power under legislation introduced in 1999. That position remained unchanged for decades, even as neighbouring countries such as Britain and France continued to use nuclear reactors as part of their electricity systems.The debate has now returned as Ireland's electricity requirements change. Data centre electricity consumption increased by 10% in 2025 compared with the previous year, while consumption from all other users increased by about 2%. Dublin had already imposed a de facto moratorium on new data centres in 2021 because the electricity grid could not keep pace with the sector's growth.One of the politicians pushing for a change is Fianna Fáil backbencher James O’Connor, who introduced a bill seeking to remove the legal barrier to nuclear power. Speaking in the Dáil in May, O’Connor said,pointing to Finland, a country with a similarly sized population that generates almost 40% of its electricity from nuclear power.Ireland has attracted major technology companies partly because of its tax regime, which has encouraged multinational companies to establish European headquarters and large operations in the country. Data centres have become an important part of that technology infrastructure, but their electricity requirements have also become a major issue for the power system.Gas made up some 40% of Ireland’s electricity in 2025, official figures show, while wind accounted for 32% and net imports via interconnectors with Britain 16%. The country has also doubled its wind generation capacity in the last ten years.Offshore wind remains another part of the government's plans, although Ireland has added relatively little offshore capacity since the Arklow project began operating 22 years ago. A decision on the country's first new offshore wind project since Arklow is due in September.O’Connor has argued that the country's decision to prohibit nuclear power has increased its exposure to energy-supply problems. However, the government has not abandoned its focus on renewable generation. Ireland now allows new data centres to proceed provided they can meet 80% of their electricity requirements from additional renewable generation within six years.Supporters of nuclear power argue that the technology could provide another source of low-carbon electricity as demand continues to grow. The Irish Academy of Engineering has estimated that a fleet of small modular reactors could supply 48% of Ireland's electricity by 2050.The country is also already indirectly exposed to nuclear-generated electricity through its electricity links with Britain, which operates nuclear power stations. A new interconnector with France is expected to be completed in 2028. France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power.said Eamonn O’Reilly, chair of the energy and climate action committee of the Irish Academy of Engineering.O’Reilly said.Small modular reactors have also attracted interest because they could be deployed at smaller sites. Dave Kirwan, managing director of Centrica Power, whose parent company has a 20% stake in Britain's existing nuclear power stations, said smaller reactors could be built at data centre sites.he said.However, nuclear power would not provide an immediate solution to Ireland's electricity challenges. Hannah Daly, professor of sustainable energy at University College Cork, said nuclear could not address the country's electricity-price, supply-security and carbon-budget challenges within the next 15 to 20 years.she said, adding thatShe also warned that presenting nuclear as a single solution could delay renewable-energy projects.Renewable-energy developers have pointed to planning and grid constraints as immediate obstacles to increasing domestic electricity generation. Kieran White, chief executive of renewables company Perigus Energy, said Ireland needed to address those problems rather than focus solely on longer-term technologies.he said.The scale of future data centre demand is another reason the nuclear debate has gained attention. Daly estimates that data centres could account for 55% of Ireland's electricity consumption by 2040 if their growth continues.Public opinion has also shifted compared with earlier years. An April opinion poll found that 43% of respondents wanted the nuclear ban removed, compared with 28% who wanted it retained. In 2021, support for and opposition to building a nuclear power station were both at 43%.Ireland's finance, public expenditure and energy ministers have all indicated that a new discussion about nuclear power is possible, while continuing to prioritise renewable energy. The outcome of O’Connor's bill remains uncertain.
Article Summary: Ireland first considered nuclear power during the 1973 oil shock. Plans for a nuclear plant on the south-east coast later faced strong opposition. The country eventually prohibited nuclear fission power under legislation introduced in 1999. That position remained unchanged for decades, even as neighbouring countries such as Britain and France continued to use nuclear reactors as part of their electricity systems.

Article Title: In 1984, NASA sent 3,301 bees into Space to test how they built honeycomb without gravity; from hitting on walls to building 200cm honeycomb; highlights of 7-day mission
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation purpose

NASA wanted to find out how bees work without gravity

The bees initially kept hitting the walls

Bees built 200 cm of honeycomb in space

Thousands of honeybees travelled into space aboard NASA 's Space Shuttle Discovery in 1984 for an experiment that sounds unusual even today. The space agency sent 3,301 bees into microgravity to see whether they could survive and, more importantly, build their famous honeycomb without the pull of gravity. The 7-day mission got off to a difficult start, with some bees crashing into the walls as they tried to fly. But within days, they adapted to their new surroundings. By the end of the mission, the bees were flying normally and had built around 200 cm of honeycomb in space.The experiment was part of the STS-41C mission and had two main goals. Researchers wanted to see how honeybees behaved and survived in microgravity. They also wanted to compare the honeycomb built in space with honeycomb made by bees on Earth.The bees were kept in specially designed enclosures with a queen bee, food and wooden frames. NASA used a mixture containing sugar, water and agar as food because ordinary liquids can form floating droplets in microgravity.The bees survived the launch, but flying in space was clearly a new experience for them. During one of the early observations, some bees tried to fly but collided with the walls of their enclosure.However, their behaviour changed as the mission continued. By the seventh day, the crew reported that the bees had adapted to zero gravity and were flying confidently.The crew wrote: “...by Day 7, comb well developed, bees seemed to adapt to 0-g pretty well. No longer trying to fly against top of box. Many actually fly from place to place.”The bees did not just survive their time in space. They also got to work. The bees in the space enclosure built about 200 cm of honeycomb during the mission. Researchers found that the honeycomb made in microgravity had some differences. The cells had smaller average diameters and thicker walls than those studied on Earth. However, the bees were still able to build cells of normal depth and use some of them to store sugar syrup.Most of the bees survived the mission. The queen also laid around 35 eggs, although the eggs did not hatch after returning to Earth. The reason for this was not known.
Article Summary: NASA wanted to find out how bees work without gravity. Bees initially kept hitting the walls as they tried to fly. But within days, they adapted to their new surroundings. By the end of the mission, the bees were flying normally and had built around 200 cm of honeycomb in space.

Article Title: 'Shocked' by hacking attacks, Bill Gates wants to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping, says: He might be surprised by how forceful I am
Article Text:
What Bill Gates wants to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping

International oversight proposal

AI hacking “should blow people's minds"

Bill Gates not the only tech leader sounding the alarm

A packed schedule of high-profile engagements

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said that he is working to arrange a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this year to propose international efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by artificial intelligence. According to a report by Reuters, Gates said that he believes China could agree to restrict potentially dangerous AI models releases if the US takes the lead. “The whole world would go along with that,” he said. Gates’ urgency is followed by recent incidents in which the AI systems from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta hacked real-world websites during cybersecurity evaluations. “These security incidents are shocking, and they should blow people’s minds,” Gates said. He warned that AI’s ability to conduct attacks, supplant jobs, and psychologically hook users represents an “evolutionary milestone” requiring unprecedented policy management.The Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist told Reuters he believes China might be willing to restrict the release of potentially dangerous AI models if the United States moved first. Gates argued that such a move by Washington could set off a global chain reaction, with the rest of the world likely to follow suit.He previously met with Xi three years ago, when he became the first foreign entrepreneur hosted by the Chinese president following the pandemic.Gates said he also wants to propose that countries jointly monitor AI systems' ability to design molecules or assist in biological attacks — an oversight measure he argued would not interfere with ongoing tech industry development. His staff are working to finalize the meeting for his next China trip, tentatively scheduled for November, according to his spokesperson.Gates said Xi "might be surprised" by how forceful he plans to be in the conversation. He credited China with taking steps to protect children from AI companion addiction, but said few global leaders are moving fast enough to get ahead of AI's potential harms. He described the current moment as unlike any past technological shift — something he called an evolutionary milestone requiring extraordinary policy management from society as a whole.In a blog post, Gates called for a new global organization to manage AI, modeled on nuclear inspections, aviation regulations, and ozone protection agreements. He said it is the “world’s top priority” to ensure AI does not widen inequality or harm vulnerable populations, ranking it above climate change and health crises.So far, the Trump administration has exercised some control over the distribution of powerful AI models, such as Anthropic's Fable 5, but most binding regulation to date has happened at the state level rather than federally.Gates struck a notably more optimistic tone about AI back in January, but his outlook has shifted since then, as he's grown increasingly concerned about AI's ability to conduct cyberattacks, displace jobs, and psychologically hook users. He pointed specifically to recent incidents in which technology from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta Platforms hacked real-world websites during what were supposed to be isolated, controlled cybersecurity evaluations. Gates called the incidents shocking, saying they should be mind-blowing to the public.Gates isn't alone in raising concerns, even as other prominent figures — including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg — have more consistently emphasized AI's benefits. Demis Hassabis, chair of Google DeepMind, has proposed a regulatory body modeled on FINRA, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, that could develop and run national-security-focused tests on AI systems.Gates said he agrees the United States should take the lead on regulation, but argued the more important, unresolved question is what specific criteria should determine when action gets taken — comparing arguments over the exact regulatory model to bickering over which restaurant to meet at while ignoring the actual subject to be discussed.Calling AI the “world's top priority"In his blog post, Gates wrote that ensuring an AI-driven future doesn't widen inequality or harm the vulnerable should be treated as the world's top priority — ranking it above both climate change and global health crises.Beyond the planned Xi meeting, Gates told Reuters he also intends to meet with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham this autumn. Not every planned engagement has gone forward, however — in February, Gates canceled a scheduled appearance in India following the U.S. release of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Gates has said previously that he did not understand the full extent of Epstein's crimes at the time he associated with him for philanthropic purposes.
Article Summary: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates wants to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping. He wants to propose international efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by artificial intelligence. Gates said he believes China could agree to restrict potentially dangerous AI models releases if the US takes the lead.
